questions.q: In Oracle's quarterly update schedule, when do non-production (Test) environments typically receive the update relative to Production?
options: At the exact same time as Production
Two weeks after Production
Two weeks before Production, giving a testing window
One full quarter before Production
questions.explain: Test environments update on the first Friday of the update month, while Production updates two weeks later on the third Friday, giving customers a testing window.

options: A group of customers sharing the same quarterly update calendar
A group of defects with the same severity
A type of configuration package
A group of legal entities sharing one ledger
questions.explain: Customers are grouped into cohorts (commonly A, B, and C) tied to different months, so Oracle doesn't push updates to every customer simultaneously.

questions.q: What is a "blackout period" in the context of Oracle's update schedule?
options: A full outage of all Oracle Cloud services
The brief window where Test and Production sit on different release levels, during which a Production-to-Test refresh can't run
The time between fit-gap analysis and configuration
A mandatory downtime for Service Requests
questions.explain: During the two-week gap between the Test update and the matching Production update, the two environments are briefly on different release levels — a blackout period for Production-to-Test refreshes.

questions.q: Why might an implementation team avoid scheduling a cutover rehearsal during a Test environment's update week?
options: Because Oracle disables all testing during updates
Because Production is unavailable during that week
Because it is against Oracle's terms of service
Because they want a stable, known configuration state during rehearsal rather than a just-changed system
questions.explain: Teams generally prefer a stable, known configuration during a major test cycle or rehearsal, so they plan around update weeks even though the update itself may not break anything.

questions.q: What matters most about the DEV/TEST/PROD distinction according to this lesson?
options: The exact names used for each environment
The discipline of using separated environments for build, test, and live use — not the specific label
That all three environments must share the same release level at all times
That only Oracle Support can access non-production environments
questions.explain: Exact instance counts and names vary by subscription and project convention; what matters functionally is the discipline of separating build, test, and live use.
